Q3390834.summary: This small ivory box is covered with finely carved scenes from both Testaments, with the life and Passion of Christ at its heart: Christ teaching, healing, raising the dead, praying in Gethsemane, and standing before his judges. Throughout, Christ appears as a beardless, long-haired young man of serene authority, a type favoured in fourth-century Italy. Made probably in Milan in the time of Saint Ambrose, it is one of the richest surviving cycles of early Christian narrative art.
facts: Its Italian name, 'Lipsanoteca', means reliquary, but it may originally have been made as a casket for other precious objects and only later used for relics.
Christ's Passion is shown without the Crucifixion itself, typical of the period, when artists still avoided depicting the cross with Christ upon it.
Old Testament scenes, such as Jonah and Daniel, appear alongside the Gospel episodes as prefigurations of salvation and resurrection.
In the nineteenth century the casket was taken apart and its panels displayed flat on a cross-shaped board; it was restored and reassembled as a box only in 1928.
Q3390834.notes: Scene identifications on the front middle register follow Watson (1981) as summarised on Wikipedia; the central scene has also been read as Christ teaching the apostles or Christ among the doctors. Worklist date '350s' changed to 'late 4th century' (one theory places it soon after 386).

met:464456.summary: Incised into a polished oval of hematite and set in a silver mount, a tall haloed Christ stands at the right while a small figure below reaches toward him, beside lines of Greek inscription. The inscriptions identify the subject as the woman healed of a flow of blood when she touched Christ's garment. Worn close to the body, the amulet invoked that healing for its owner.
facts: The Met notes that hematite was believed to stop the flow of blood, and was a favourite stone for amulets concerned with women's reproductive health.
On the reverse a woman stands in the orant (prayer) pose.
It was a gift of J. Pierpont Morgan in 1917.
met:464456.notes: The inscription is not transcribed here because it was not verified letter by letter. The kneeling woman is small and unclear in the photograph.

Q3111703.summary: Here Christ reigns from the cross rather than suffering upon it: eyes open, head upright, he wears a long royal tunic richly painted with floral motifs. This type of 'Majestat' presents the crucified Lord as the King of Glory, victorious over death, and the Batlló Majesty is the finest and best-preserved example of it.
facts: It takes its name from Enric Batlló, who gave it to the Diputació de Barcelona as a long-term loan to the museum in 1914.
Its paint survives remarkably well, including vivid red from cinnabar and blue from lapis lazuli — costly pigments — on a tunic whose motifs recall luxurious Byzantine and Hispano-Moorish silks.
Catalan Majestats are related to the famous Volto Santo of Lucca, a venerated robed crucifix that inspired copies across Europe.
The tunic (colobium) recalls early Eastern images of the crucified Christ, before the loincloth became standard in Western art.

Q1199503.summary: In this late work, Corinth paints the Crucifixion in violent reds, as if the whole scene were soaked in blood and fire. A soldier drives the lance into Christ's side, another lifts the vinegar-soaked sponge, and the mourning Virgin and Saint John press close to a Christ whose body is built from thick, slashing strokes of brush and palette knife. Painted three years before the artist's death, it is one of the most intense religious paintings of the Weimar years.
facts: Corinth suffered a serious stroke in December 1911 that left him partly paralysed on his left side; afterwards his style loosened and took on many Expressionist qualities.
Between Christ's outstretched arms the sun blazes with sharp rays, and sky, lake and sun are all drenched in red; Corinth painted on wood rather than canvas, in the manner of old German altarpieces.
Corinth trained as a realist and Impressionist, but works like this made him an important bridge to German Expressionism.
